messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Mehta was 37 when he came for treatment, a married Indian American psychologist who was embarrassed by how much effort it now took to get through an ordinary day. The event he returned to in fragments had happened eight months earlier, when he and his wife were leaving an evening community program at a cultural center in the city. It was already dark. As they moved toward the parking area, gunfire erupted nearby and people scattered in confused waves, ducking behind cars and concrete planters. Arjun could remember the metallic crack of the shots far more clearly than anything visual. What stayed with him was the instant collapse of order: bodies pushing, his wife pulled out of his reach for several seconds, the sickening knowledge that he could not control where to run, who was safe, or whether another shot was coming. By the time they got home, he had begun to feel that something essential had shifted. He was not only shaken by what had happened; he had come to believe that the world itself had revealed its true nature as violently unsafe, and that when danger came, he was powerless to stop bad things from happening.

In the first weeks after the attack, nighttime became especially difficult. Waking in the dark, even in his own bedroom, brought back the same bodily jolt he had felt in the parking lot, as if the loss of control were happening again before he had fully opened his eyes. Sharp sounds outside—an engine backfiring, construction noise, anything resembling a gunshot—could stop him in place. In those moments he found his mind snapping to the same conclusions: this is what the world is really like, danger can break in anywhere, and he cannot protect himself or the people he loves. He was disturbed, too, by what he saw in himself. He had spent years helping patients think clearly under stress, and now he found himself reacting before he could reason. The person he had become felt unrecognizable to him.

Those reactions began shaping his days. At the hospital clinic where he worked, he started turning down cases he expected to be emotionally intense, telling colleagues he needed to protect his bandwidth. He left evening meetings early so he would not have to walk to the parking garage after dark. If there was a choice between a manageable inconvenience and anything that felt potentially stressful, he avoided the stressor. When a loud sound from the street cut through a session, he noticed his attention drifting away from the patient into an inward, unreal space where he did not have to be present for the tension in his body. At home he began pouring a drink most nights before bed, and on some nights added leftover medication from an old prescription, hoping to blunt the edgy anticipation that came with darkness. The more convinced he became that the world was dangerous and that he was no longer the steady, capable man he used to be, the more these habits made sense to him as necessary ways of getting through.

But over the following months those ways of coping deepened the very beliefs that frightened him. Each avoided errand, each refusal to stay out after sunset, seemed to confirm that ordinary life really was too dangerous to manage. When he drifted off mentally during tense moments, he felt ashamed afterward, reading it as proof that he could no longer face reality directly. Drinking and medicating gave temporary relief, yet the next morning he often woke groggy in the dark before dawn, disoriented and immediately on edge. That state made him feel even less in control, strengthening his conviction that bad things could happen to him at any moment and that he would be helpless again.

The cycle tightened around specific triggers. Because he increasingly organized his life around avoiding stress, his world became narrower and more brittle; small disruptions hit him harder. A late-night phone alert, fireworks in the distance, or waking to a dark room after his wife had already gone downstairs could set off an outsized surge of alarm. He noticed that after evenings of drinking, ordinary nighttime sounds seemed more menacing, and his startled response to anything like gunfire was quicker, not less. Even at work, in an office where he once felt grounded, he found himself scanning for exits when a door slammed in the hallway. He would retreat into detached daydreaming after these moments, or cancel the rest of his schedule if he could, because the trigger had already convinced him that the day was no longer safe.

His marriage had begun to feel the effects. His wife had stopped asking him to join friends for dinners or concerts after dark because he almost always found a reason not to go. He hated the shrinking look of concern on her face when he checked locks repeatedly before bed, yet he also felt certain that if he relaxed, he would be failing to prevent the next catastrophe. What finally brought him in was a recent incident at the clinic: a car backfired outside, and he lost the thread of a patient’s disclosure completely, staring past her and feeling himself disappear into that private, far-off place. He was ashamed that his patients now encountered the version of him he barely recognized. Sitting in treatment, he said he was afraid this was permanent—that he had learned something terrible and true about the world and about himself—but he was also hoping, cautiously, that he might not always have to live as though the gunshots were about to start again.
